summary: The SIP Alert-Info header field points to a ring tone or similar alerting signal. This document defines URNs for it, so a caller or network can name a standard kind of alert instead of linking to a specific sound file.

eli5.summary: Instead of sending a particular ringtone file, a phone call can say ring like an emergency or like a normal call, by a standard name.

questions: how to name ringtones in sip
what is the alert urn namespace
how do sip ring tones work
subtitle: Standard names for ring tones and other alert signals in SIP, so the receiving phone chooses how to render them.

tldr.problem: The SIP Alert-Info header normally points to a specific sound file, which ties the alert to one rendering and has led to vendor-specific conventions that only work when one vendor supplies both PBX and phone.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7462 defines the "alert" URN namespace of the form urn:alert:category:indication, with a registry of standard values, private extensions and rules for combining several URNs in priority order.
tldr.outcome: A sender can say what kind of alert it means, such as call waiting or an external caller, and the receiver picks the tone, vibration or display. The RFC also updates RFC 3261 to allow Alert-Info in non-100 provisional responses.

today: RFC 7462 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3261, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Alert-Info URLs
sections.content:
In the Session Initiation Protocol (RFC 3261), the Alert-Info header field suggests a ring tone or ringback tone by giving a URI, most commonly an HTTP URL of an audio file. That hinders interoperability. The meaning of the tone may be country- or vendor-specific, a deaf or hard-of-hearing user may not sense an audio file, and the tone is no use to automata.

Fixed URLs with special meanings do not fully fix it, because vendors invent different conventions. The RFC lists three ways to signal an external caller, for example <file://ring.pcm>;alert=external, <file://external.ring.pcm> and <sip:external-ringtone@example.com>. As a result, the header only works when one vendor supplies both PBX and phone.

The answer is a URN namespace named alert. A URN is a name, not a download, so there is nothing to fetch, no formatting or security issue from dereferencing, and the device can store the tone locally. The downside is that a recipient that does not understand the URN can only render a default tone. The document lists 20 requirements, such as specifying alerts by name rather than by value, allowing extension by uncoordinated organizations, giving only an indication and not a negotiation, and letting a receiver ignore URNs it does not understand.
sections.eli5: A link to a sound file is like telling a friend to play track 5 of your CD. Your friend may not own the CD. A name like 'urgent' lets their own phone choose a fitting sound.

sections.title: Updates to RFC 3261
sections.content:
This RFC formally updates RFC 3261 in two ways. First, Alert-Info is now allowed in any non-100 provisional response to an INVITE. Before, it was only permitted in 180 (Ringing) responses, but telephony often signals other situations with tones too, such as 181 (Call Is Being Forwarded) and 182 (Call Is Being Queued). The first paragraph of Section 20.4 of RFC 3261 is replaced: in an INVITE the header specifies an alternative ring tone to the UAS, and in a non-100 provisional response it specifies an alternative ringback tone to the UAC.

Second, a SIP proxy MAY add or remove an Alert-Info header field, and MAY add or remove its values, in a request or a non-100 provisional response.

Compatibility is expected to be fine. Devices that do not understand an alert URN should ignore it, and multiple Alert-Info values were already syntactically allowed.
sections.eli5: Before, a call could only say 'ring like this' at one moment. Now it can also say 'ring like this' while the call is being forwarded or put in a queue, and helpers along the way can add or remove those hints.

sections.title: The alert URN Syntax
sections.content:
An alert URN has the general form urn:alert:<alert-category>:<alert-indication>. The category is the first colon-separated part, and the indication is one or more further parts, called alert-ind-parts. The structure is hierarchical, so removing the last part gives a shorter URN with a less specific meaning.

Labels MUST be Non-Reserved LDH labels, which are ordinary ASCII labels. Registered URNs MUST be transmitted exactly as registered, including case, while comparison for equivalence is case-insensitive. A private name has the form label@provider.

One URN does not describe a whole signal, only one characteristic of it. The full request is a sequence of URNs in priority order, with earlier ones more important. The scope is public and global. Standard values are held in the IANA registry 'Alert URN Identifiers' under Specification Required, and provider names in the 'Alert URN Providers' registry under First Come First Served, which starts with one entry, example.
sections.eli5: An alert name is like a street address written from big to small: first the kind of alert, then the exact type. Cut off the end and you get a vaguer address.

sections.title: Categories and Standard Values
sections.content:
Six categories are defined, and each has a default value that is essentially a no-operation and should be treated as if no URN for that category were present. That default is useful when header parameters need an Alert-Info to be present but no special tone is wanted, as in RFC 7463.

  • service: normal (default), call-waiting, forward, recall:callback, recall:hold, recall:transfer.
  • source: unclassified (default), internal, external, friend, family. These are usually inserted by a proxy acting for the recipient.
  • priority: normal (default), low, high.
  • duration: normal (default), short, long.
  • delay: none (default), yes.
  • locale: default (default) or country:<ISO 3166-1 country code>, for example urn:alert:locale:country:za for South African ringback tones.

The use cases behind these values include PBX tones such as internal, external, priority, short ('abbreviated ringing' or 'zip tone') and delayed, and service tones such as call waiting, transfer recall (RFC 5589) and auto callback (RFC 6910).
sections.eli5: There are six dials: what service is happening, who is calling, how urgent, how long, whether to wait a moment, and which country's ring to use. Each dial rests on 'normal' until someone turns it.

sections.title: Extending the Namespace
sections.content:
The namespace is extensible at any level. A new top-level entry creates a category, a second-level entry creates a value in an existing category, and deeper entries subdivide existing values. A new category must be independent of existing ones, and a new identifier must be a refinement of its parent with no semantic overlap with its siblings.

Private extensions use the label@provider form and are not registered with IANA. The organization that owns the provider value defines the meaning of its private names and of the plain labels that follow them, up to the next private name, and is responsible for keeping that meaning stable. An organization obtains its provider value by registering it with IANA. A private extension MUST NOT duplicate any standard URN or any private extension the organization knows about.

Examples use the provider example: urn:alert:service:call-waiting:abc@example subsets a standard value, urn:alert:service:ghi@example adds a new service, and urn:alert:jkl@example:a1 adds a whole new category. Another organization can refine a private URN further, as in urn:alert:distinctive@foo:short-short@bar.
sections.eli5: Anyone can add new words to the alert dictionary, but company-made words carry the company's name tag, like 'Rex's special'. Only that company decides what its word means.

sections.title: Combining Several URNs
sections.content:
Several URNs can appear in one or more Alert-Info header fields. For instance, <urn:alert:source:internal>, <urn:alert:priority:high> indicates an internal, priority call. The sender may include redundant or contradictory URNs, and an earlier URN wins over a later contradictory one. Adding a URN at the start requires a feature value, and adding it at the end only suggests one.

The receiving UA may ignore URNs it does not recognize or cannot render. It MUST follow three rules. (a) Each URN has precedence over all that follow it. (b) If a URN cannot be given effect, the UA repeatedly removes its final part until a recognized URN results, or ignores the URN if nothing is left. (c) If several signals are equally effective, the least specific one is chosen, though a more specific one may be chosen using information from the SIP message, such as a Priority: urgent header field. Local policy and UA status, such as an active call, can change the choice.

Section 12 gives a non-normative sorting algorithm. Each category has a feature tree, each signal has a position in every tree, and each URN in turn removes incompatible signals and sorts the rest by how much of the URN they express. The first remaining signal is chosen. Its five worked examples show, for instance, that if source:internal comes before priority:low and no signal matches both, the priority URN cannot take effect.
sections.eli5: It is like ordering pizza with a list of wishes, most important first. The kitchen gives you the best match for the first wish, then tries to honour the next wish only if it does not spoil the first.

sections.title: User Agent and Proxy Behaviour
sections.content:
A SIP user agent MAY add alert URNs to a request or a 1xx response other than 100. On receiving them, it matches them to a signal it can render using the rules above. It MUST produce a rendering from the URIs it can understand and act on, ignore the others, and SHOULD provide some alert unless instructed otherwise, for example by a Replaces or Joins header field, local policy or the user. Later provisional responses in the same dialog are treated independently, and the UA SHOULD render the last received value.

A proxy MAY add or remove the header and its values when it needs to change the information about the call. The RFC gives four reasons: to add indications based on what the proxy knows, such as an external source or a Priority: urgent header; to show that a service is invoked at this end; to remove deceptive indications from untrusted sources; and to remove indications that should be suppressed for privacy.

In the RFC's example, a proxy adds both a network audio resource and the call-waiting URN to a 180 Ringing response, and the UAC may render either or both.
sections.eli5: The phone follows the hints it understands and ignores the rest, and it should still ring. A helper in the middle can add helpful hints or erase sneaky ones.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
As an identifier, the alert URN raises no particular security issues, because the indications are meant to be well known. The concern is privacy: specific indications can reveal facts about the source UA, such as its nature, its dialog state or services started at its end. Call waiting and call forwarding can reveal dialog state.

Sending such indications SHALL always require authorization on behalf of the source UA's user, usually via configured policy, and authorization SHALL NOT assume the recipients are limited without specific information about the SIP transaction. A UA MAY ignore undesirable indications, and a proxy acting for a UA MAY add or delete indications for the same reasons. S/MIME MAY be used to protect the indications end to end, and UAs that implement them SHOULD also implement SIP over TLS and the sips: scheme.
sections.eli5: A ring hint can give away secrets, like that you are already on another call. So a phone should only share these hints when its owner allows it.

SIP/2.0 180 Ringing
Alert-Info: <http://www.example.com/sound/moo.wav>,
             <urn:alert:service:call-waiting>
To: Bob <sip:bob@biloxi.example.com>;tag=a6c85cf
From: Alice <sip:alice@atlanta.example.com>;tag=1928301774
CSeq: 314159 INVITE
Content-Length: 0
